entries.title: List comprehensions
entries.what: `[e for x in xs if c]` builds a vector, a matrix (when every `e` is a vector of one length) or a list of strings, as Python's does. More `for`s nest, the first outermost, and the `for` takes any head a `for` statement takes. The parser writes it as the loop it stands for, so every engine runs it.
entries.when: Instead of a `for` loop that fills a preallocated array or appends under an `if`.

squares = [i * i for i to 5]
show evens, squares
test "a comprehension keeps what its if holds for" {
    assert_allclose(squares, [0.0, 1.0, 4.0, 9.0, 16.0], 0.0)
}

entries.title: Map comprehensions
entries.what: `{k: v for x in xs if c}` builds a map, Python's dict comprehension, with the same heads and filters as a list comprehension. A key seen again keeps its first place and takes the later value. A brace in an expression is only this form: a set literal `{x, y}` is refused with a pointer to `unique`.

entries.title: Generator arguments and short-circuit all/any

entries.title: The if-expression
entries.what: `a if c else b` is `a` when `c` holds and `b` otherwise; only the chosen side is computed. It binds loosest of all operators, as in Python, so `a if c else b if d else e` chains.

entries.title: Slices
entries.what: `a[lo:hi:s]`, `A[i, :]`, `A[:, j]` and `A[r0:r1, c0:c1]` select a block of an array of rank up to 4. The result is a copy, never a view; a plain index drops its axis. Bounds are not clamped: a range past the end stops the run with its line, where NumPy would clamp. A negative step walks back, as Python's: `a[::-1]` is `a` back to front, `a[4:1:-1]` is a[4], a[3], a[2], `A[:, ::-1]` reverses the columns.
entries.when: Instead of a copy loop over part of an array, and instead of `slab` for a row or a plane.

example.code:

test "a slice is a copy" {
    assert_near(a[1], 1.0, 0.0)
    assert_allclose(A[:, 1], [2.0, 5.0], 0.0)
    assert_allclose(a[4:1:-1], [4.0, 3.0, 2.0], 0.0)
}

entries.title: Operators: ^, %, //, @, and, or
entries.what: `x ^ y` is `pow(x, y)`, right-associative and tighter than a unary minus (`-2 ^ 2` is -4). `a % b` is the floored remainder and `a // b` the floored quotient, Python's rules. `@` is the matrix product (NumPy's matmul). `and` and `or` short-circuit in every engine, so `j > 0 and a[j - 1] > v` never reads `a[-1]`. `+` of two arrays adds them element by element; it does not join them as Python's lists, and `[1.0] + row` (a one-element literal beside an array, or literals of different lengths) is refused with a note naming `concat`.
entries.when: Instead of `pow` calls, `mod` (C's fmod, which takes the sign of `a`), and nested `if`s that guard an index.

example.code:
p = 2.0 ^ 3.0 ^ 2.0
neg = -2.0 ^ 2.0
r = -7.0 % 3.0
q = 7.0 // -2.0
A = [[1.0, 2.0], [3.0, 4.0]]
y = A @ [1.0, 1.0]
a = [5.0]
safe = len(a) > 1 and a[1] > 0.0
show p, neg, r, q, y, safe
test "power, floored division and modulo, matmul, short circuit" {
    assert_near(p, 512.0, 0.0)
    assert_near(neg, -4.0, 0.0)
    assert_near(r, 2.0, 0.0)
    assert_near(q, -4.0, 0.0)
    assert_allclose(y, [3.0, 7.0], 0.0)
}

entries.what: `fn(x) -> expr` is a function value with a single-expression body, which may read the program's variables. Assign it, pass it, call it through a parameter. The body may hold a comprehension, a map comprehension, a generator argument or an if-expression (`encode = fn(text) -> [stoi[c] for c in text]`). entries.title: Closures: lambdas that capture
entries.what: A lambda written inside a def reads the def's locals and parameters, and holds the values they had when it was made: a later assignment does not reach it. Bind it to a name and call it, or pass it to a def. It cannot be returned, stored in an array, record or map, or assign a name it captured. The compiled engines lift it to a def whose trailing parameters are the captured values, and specialize the def it is passed to, so no closure is allocated and every call is direct.

entries.title: format specs: Python's flags
entries.what: A spec is Python's: `[[fill]align][sign][0][width][,|_][.precision][type]`, the type one of `e E f F g G d %` or none (the repr). `{x:06.2f}` is `-01.50`, `{x:+.3e}` shows the sign, `{x:*^9.2f}` centers with `*`, `{n:,}` groups thousands, `{p:.1%}` is a percent, `{x:G}` is upper case; an Int takes the same flags. A width or precision can be a value, as in Python: `{name:>{w}}`, `{x:.{p}f}`, `fmt(x, f".{p}g")`. `fmt(x, spec)` reads the same specs. `#`, `z`, `n` and the integer bases are refused with a message.
entries.when: Instead of building a field by hand with rjust, a sign test or upper(fmt(x, "g")), or a spec string per width.

example.code:
x = -1.5

entries.title: Float32, IEEE single precision

entries.title: Maps

entries.title: Complex numbers: Cplx and CArr
entries.what: The `i` suffix makes an imaginary literal (`3.0 + 4.0i`); complex scalars have full arithmetic with real promotion, `re`, `im`, `conj`, `abs` and complex `exp`, `log`, `sqrt`, `sin`, `cos`, `tan`. `czeros(n)` or a literal with a complex element makes a complex array (`CArr`), packed as interleaved doubles. entries.title: The NumPy array vocabulary

entries.title: Masks, `where`, `extract` and `putmask`
entries.what: A comparison with an array on either side gives a mask of 1.0 and 0.0. `where(m, a, b)` picks from `a` or `b` and broadcasts all three; `extract(m, a)` is NumPy's `a[mask]`, `putmask(a, m, v)` is `a[mask] = v` in place, `flatnonzero(m)` gives the positions, and `count_nonzero`, `any` and `all` read a mask. `if a == b` on arrays is refused with a note to write `all(a == b)`.

entries.title: Sums in a loop's order: `sum(a, ordered=true)`
entries.what: `sum(a, ordered=true)` adds every element left to right from 0.0, the order of a Fortran or C loop, where `sum(a)` adds in NumPy's pairwise order. The two can differ in the last digits (or more, when large terms cancel). `dot` and `prod` always go left to right; `dot(u, v, ordered=true)` says so in the code and changes nothing. The value is `true` or `false` as written, and the option takes no `axis=`.
entries.when: When a port must match a reference written with loops to its printed digits: write the reduction as `sum(x, ordered=true)` or `dot(u, v)` instead of the loop that adds one element per pass.

example.code:

# both 1.0s; a loop loses only the first, since -1.0e16 cancels 1.0e16 before
# the second 1.0 comes.
x = [1.0e16, 1.0, -1.0e16, 1.0, 3.0, 1.0e-3, 7.0, 2.0, 1.0, 1.0]
loop = 0.0
for i to len(x) {
    loop += x[i]
}
show sum(x), sum(x, ordered=true), loop
test "the ordered sum is the loop's, to the bit" {
    assert_true(sum(x, ordered=true) == loop)
    assert_true(dot(x, x, ordered=true) == dot(x, x))
}

entries.title: Test blocks

entries.title: Holds: claims checked while the program runs
entries.what: A `hold` in a debug lens (`<module>.debug`, or an inline `debug { }` block) is an assertion with a sentence, checked at a step (`hold at update ...`) or after every pass of a def's loops. `a == b within tol` compares with a tolerance, over every element for arrays. A hold may read the def's variables and call pure builtins. A failed hold goes into the story and makes the run exit nonzero (`1 hold FAILED`); the printed output does not change. `viv run --release` and `-DVIV_RELEASE` skip them.

entries.title: Contracts: integrate and find_root
entries.what: `integrate(f, a, b)` and `find_root(f, a, b)` are named for the problem, not a method. Each is a `contract` with three methods from different families (Gauss-Legendre, adaptive Simpson and Romberg; a safeguarded secant, bisection and Illinois). A call runs the default (Gauss, the secant); `using q_romberg` picks another; `using every method` solves by all three, stops if one is farther than relative 1e-8 from their median, and returns the median. `find_root` first asserts that f changes sign on [a, b]. They are in lang/viv/std/contracts.viv, brought in with `#! use lang/viv/std/contracts`.
entries.when: For a quadrature or a root: call the default, and run every method in a test where a wrong answer would go unnoticed.

PASS find_root and integrate agree with the closed forms
PASS every method agrees

entries.title: Declaring a contract and its methods
entries.what: `contract name(params) -> out: Type, ... { ... }` names a problem: `intent "..."` says what it computes, `methods a, b` lists the defs that solve it (or a block of `label: a, b` lines, groups that `using every <label> method` runs; the first, or the `default`, is the one a call runs), and `agree out within relative T`, `within absolute T` or `exactly` says what two methods must agree on, T one number or one name (relative: |a - b| <= T max(1, |reference|)). A method's parameters beyond the contract's are its settings, with defaults in its own signature; a top-level `settings b(tol = 1e-12)` gives them wherever b runs. A program chooses once at the top level: `using name = b`, `using name = sel` (a variable, such as a program parameter), or `using name = every method`, which runs them all and stops at the first disagreement; following calls run that choice. `name(...) using b` is a one-off for one call; `viv run --using name=b` sets the start. The compiler checks every method's parameters, types, settings and number of results against the contract. It compiles to an enum, a selection variable and a def, so all three engines run it.
entries.when: Wherever two algorithms compute the same thing (eigensolvers, quadratures, integral engines): declare the contract, call the default, and run every method in the tests.

entries.title: Method registries and the sweep
entries.what: A registry is an array of function values, `[q_gauss, q_romberg]`, returned from a def or held in a variable. `sweep(methods, f, a, b)` (std/contracts) runs every method in it, asserts that the worst deviation from the median is below 1e-8 (1 + |median|), and returns the median; `sweep_spread(methods, f, a, b, out)` writes each result into `out` and returns the worst deviation, without asserting. Adding a method is adding its name to the array. The compiled engines call through a function pointer. `spectrum_sym(A, vals)` is the builtin form: it checks that A is symmetric and computes the spectrum by cyclic Jacobi and by Householder plus QL, and stops on dissent; release mode runs QL only.
entries.when: Wherever two or more algorithms compute the same thing (ERIs, J/K builders, quadratures, eigensolvers): register them and sweep, instead of writing one driver per method or comparing by hand in a notebook.

example.code:
from lang.viv.std.contracts import q_gauss, q_romberg, sweep, sweep_spread
# A registry is an array of function values; `sweep` runs every method in it
# and stops the run if they disagree.
def q_midpoint(f, a, b) {
    n = 2000.0
    h = (b - a) / n
    s = 0.0
    for k to n {
        s = s + f(a + (k + 0.5) * h)
    }
    return s * h
}

def loose_methods() {
    return [q_gauss, q_romberg, q_midpoint]
}

methods = [q_gauss, q_romberg]
area = sweep(methods, fn(x) -> exp(x), 0.0, 1.0)
out = zeros(3)
worst = sweep_spread(loose_methods(), fn(x) -> exp(x), 0.0, 1.0, out)
show area, worst
A = [[2.0, 1.0], [1.0, 2.0]]
vals = zeros(2)
spectrum_sym(A, vals)
show vals
test "the registry agrees on the integral of exp from 0 to 1" {
    assert_near(area, exp(1.0) - 1.0, 1.0e-12)
    assert_lt(worst, 1.0e-6)
    assert_allclose(vals, [1.0, 3.0], 1.0e-12)
}

# SPDX-FileCopyrightText: 2026 The Viv authors

area: 1.71828  worst: 1.78988e-08

entries.title: Phrases held to exact values: viv check --phrases
entries.what: `viv check --phrases <file>` finds every phrase with a closed form (integrals, derivatives, polynomial roots of degree 1 to 3, sums, norms and traces of written-out arrays), computes its exact value with lib/cas, and compares it with the number the program computes, within a tolerance set by the method. It prints the exact value, how it was found (an antiderivative whose derivative is checked against the integrand; the quadratic formula), the numeric value, and the math as TeX. A phrase it cannot handle (a hole that reads a value computed at run time, a polynomial of degree 4) is reported as refused, never passed. A phrase that disagrees makes it exit 1. `--json` prints the records; `--emit out.viv` writes the check program it runs.

entries.title: What the compiler refuses instead of guessing
entries.what: The front end stops with a located error, in every engine, where another language would pick a meaning: `2x` (write `2 * x`); `if a == b` on arrays (a comparison of arrays is a mask; write `all(a == b)`); a number or an array as a condition; `true + 1.0`; a call with the wrong argument count; an unknown name; a def and a top-level variable with one name; a format outside `[width][.precision]e|f|g|d`; a map that stores a number key and a string key. At run time an index or slice outside its array stops the run with its line (`index 5 out of bounds for dimension 0 (size 3)`); nothing is clamped or wrapped.

entries.title: viv check: the checks a run makes, without running
entries.what: `viv check <file>` runs the compiler's front end (what the C and wasm builds share) and the interpreter's own checks, and nothing else. It is silent with exit 0 when the program would run, and prints located diagnostics with exit 1 when not. `--json` prints them as one JSON object; `--use` and `--set` work as for `viv run`; a Python file is translated by py2viv first. `--phrases` is a different check (check-phrases-certificates).
entries.when: After every edit, before a long run, and in an agent's loop: it is fast and gives the same errors the engines would.

entries.title: Problem posts: tests that fail until solved

A solution post (`kind: solution`, `solves: <slug>`) keeps every test word for word and passes them.

areas.what: what a program says about itself beside its code

entries.title: The intent lens: what each def is for, in a file beside the code
entries.what: `<module>.intent` holds one block per def, headed by the def's name and its body hash: `what`, `how` and `why` lines, a glossary line per variable (`x  the current estimate`), and the def's steps as an outline with the control words `repeat until ...`, `if ...`, `for each ...`. The same entries can be written inline as `#|`, `#||`, `#|||` and `#:` comments above the def; each anchor has one home, and `viv lens move --to-file|--to-inline` moves them. `viv lens init` writes a skeleton with every def, step and hash; `viv lens check` fails on a stale entry, a public def with no `what`, a step with no text, an outline whose nesting differs from the code, or a number in the text with no `[test "..."]` citation.
entries.when: For every library def another person or agent will read or change. The code file stays free of prose, and the check keeps the prose from drifting from the code.

entries.title: Intent at the def, step and statement level
entries.what: An intent entry explains a def (`what`, `how`, `why`, the glossary), each of its steps (one line of text, and `why` and `how` lines under it), and single statements: `= x  <text>` under a step explains the first statement of that step that assigns `x`, `= f()` the first that calls `f`, `#k` the k-th, and `>` adds a paragraph. An anchor that names no statement fails `viv lens check`.
entries.when: Explain a statement when the line alone does not say its purpose or its physical meaning. Restating the code in words is not an explanation.

entries.title: Stamps: an entry records the code it was written for
entries.what: Each `.intent` and `.debug` entry carries `@<body hash>`, the hash `viv hash` prints for the def's body (it ignores formatting and the def's name). When the body changes, the entry is stale: `viv lens check` reports it with the structural diff and fails. `viv lens stamp <file> <def>` records that the entry was re-read and is right for the new body. Inline entries are stamped by a `#@ <hash>` line.
entries.when: After editing a def, re-read its entry, fix it, then stamp it. Do not stamp without reading: the stamp is the record that the text matches the code.

entries.title: viv digits: which printed digits are real
entries.what: `viv digits <file>` runs the program in the interpreter once as written, then again with its floating-point evaluation perturbed, and gives for every printed number the leading significant digits that stay the same, with a `|` where they stop. The perturbations, each switchable: the order of every built-in reduction (`sum`, `dot`, the sums of `@`: pairwise, left to right, reversed, random), FMA contraction of `a*b + c`, and Monte Carlo arithmetic as Verificarlo does it (noise of half an ulp on each `+ - * /`, digits `-log10(sigma/|mu|)` over the samples). It then perturbs the most-executed lines one at a time and says which printed numbers each one moves. A whole result with no rounding error (an index, a size) is left exact. `--json` and `-o` write the report the explorer shows; `vipyr.digits` runs it from Python.
entries.when: To learn how many digits of a result to quote, and which lines lose the rest, without knowing the exact answer.

example.code:
# 1 - cos(x) cancels: what is left of cos(x)'s rounding error decides the digits
x = 1.0e-6
naive = 1.0 - cos(x)
s = sin(x / 2.0)
good = 2.0 * s * s
print("1 - cos(x) = ", naive)
print("2 sin(x/2)^2 = ", good)
test "the two agree to the digits the subtraction keeps" {
    assert_true(abs(naive - good) < 1.0e-3 * good)
}

# SPDX-License-Identifier: MIT OR Apache-2.0
# SPDX-FileCopyrightText: 2026 The Viv authors

entries.title: The memory lens: what each def does with its arrays
entries.what: `viv view <file> --lens memory` prints, for each def, what the compiler infers: which parameters it writes in place (the caller sees the change), which it only reads, what it returns, and what a loop pass keeps or frees. Nothing in it is written by hand. A `<module>.memory` file holds the one fact the compiler takes on trust: a `disjoint` pin saying a `parallel for` writes different elements on every pass, which checked builds verify while they run.

entries.title: The architecture lens: layers, budgets and multi-paths

entries.title: Run a program in the interpreter
entries.what: `viv run f.viv` runs the program in the tree-walking interpreter, the same one the browser workbench runs. `-q` drops the `__graph__`, `__trace__`, `__steps__` and `__story__` lines the debug lens prints; `--release` makes `release_mode()` true, so a contract runs one method instead of sweeping; `--json` writes the errors and the failed-assert summary to stderr as one JSON object; `--use p.viv` puts a prelude before the program; `--set NAME=value` replaces a top-level `NAME = <number>` line before the run. A failed assert or hold makes the exit status 1. A `.py` file, or one that starts with `#! lang python`, is translated by py2viv first. The interpreter stops a run past 2e9 steps, its guard against a hung loop; `VIV_STEP_BUDGET=2e10 viv run f.viv` raises the limit for a long run that is not a hang.
entries.when: To try a change without a C compiler, to sweep a parameter with `--set` instead of editing the file, and to give a tool or a model the errors as JSON.

    total += h * x * x
}

test "the midpoint rule is close to 1/3" {

}

entries.title: Compile to C or to wasm
entries.what: `viv f.viv -o f.c` writes one C99 file that holds the program and the runtime it needs; `viv f.viv -o f.wasm` writes a WebAssembly module from the direct wasm backend, which `tools/run-wasm.mjs` runs in node. `--emit tokens`, `--emit ast` and `--emit ir` print the lexer's tokens, the syntax tree or the IR (each node with its content hash) and stop; the IR shows the call a form becomes, such as `2.0 ^ 3`, which is a call of `pow`. The C is built with any C compiler (`cc -O2 f.c -lm`), and prints what the interpreter prints, byte for byte.

entries.title: The program graph and the explorer
entries.what: `viv graph f.viv` prints the program as a graph of defs, the steps inside them and the loops that hold them, with each step's inputs and outputs. `--json` is the graph for tools, `--bundle` adds the program as run, its line table, the intent and the debug lens (what the /explore page loads), `--run` runs the program as the explorer does, and `--svg [-o out.svg]` draws the whole program with lib/graphdraw. The explorer page runs the program in your browser and places each moment of the run in this graph, step by step.
entries.when: To see the structure of a program you did not write before reading its code, and to check that the steps you named give each phase the inputs and outputs you meant.

entries.what: This repository has no `viv fmt`. entries.title: Math in figure labels
entries.what: A figure label's `$...$` parts are TeX, set as math by `viv plot` and by the site's charts alike: Greek letters, `^` and `_`, `\frac`, `\sqrt`, accents, `\mathrm` and `\text`, operator names such as `\log` set upright, `\sum` and `\int`, `\left(` `\right)`, the spacing commands and the common relations and operators. Titles, axis labels, legend entries, ticks and label marks all take it; text outside the dollars stays as it is, and `\$` is a dollar sign. An unknown command makes `viv plot` fail with the record's line and the column in the label. In a Viv string a backslash is written `\\`.

entries.title: Export a program as one C file and a Python wrapper
entries.what: `viv export p.export.toml` reads a manifest that names a program's files, its decks, its parameters and its results, and writes `p.c` (the program and its runtime, which `cc -shared` builds into a library), `p.h`, `p.py` (a ctypes wrapper with a typed `run`), a README and a test, by default into `target/export/p`. A run of the library gives the bits a run of the program gives; an error in it raises a Python exception with Viv's message and line, and the next run works. A manifest with `kind = "kernels"` and `[kernels.<name>]` tables exports several defs instead, each a C entry point and a Python function with the def's signature (complex numbers and several results included), after a module initialization that runs once.

entries.title: The CUDA C of a program's GPU kernels
entries.what: `viv cuda p.viv -o p.cu` writes one CUDA C file: Viv's libm marked for the device, a `__global__` function for each `kernel def` and for each `parallel for` whose body can run on a GPU, and an `extern "C"` launcher for each that computes the grid as the emulator does (the default, or the kernel's `schedule` line), copies the arrays to the device, launches and copies the written ones back. A `parallel for` that cannot be a kernel is listed at the end of the file with the reason. The file is meant for nvcc with `-fmad=false -prec-div=true -prec-sqrt=true -ftz=false`. `--set NAME=value` sets a global constant first, as in a run, so one source gives a file per block shape or tile size.

A translated program behaves as CPython with NumPy runs it, or py2viv refuses it, listing every construct outside the subset at its Python line and column with what to write instead. `def test_x():` becomes a `test` block, and a run-time error is reported at the Python line it came from.

entries.title: The Python and Viv pairs
entries.what: study/compare holds the same small programs in Python and in Viv, topic by topic (basics, strings, maps, records, autodiff, ml, numerics, plotting and more), each pair split into matching `# @@` regions. `study/compare/check.sh` lints them, runs both sides and requires the same printed text, checks each pair's `.gen.json` (which the /compare pages are built from) is current, and runs the three engines; measure.py keeps each measured pair's line and lookup counts current in its notes.
entries.when: To see how a Python idiom is written in Viv before writing it, and to measure what a language change saves.
entries.noExample: a harness over study/compare; run study/compare/check.sh

entries.title: The algorithms harness
entries.what: `python3 tools/algo/check.py` checks lib/algo's specification (lib/algo/algo.spec: each algorithm's postconditions, stability and complexity bound) and the test programs generated from it; `--run` runs each implementation on generated cases, recomputes every property in Python, compares with Python and NumPy, counts comparisons against the bound and runs the three engines. It is part of www's `npm run check`.
entries.when: Before adding a sort, search or set algorithm to lib/algo, or when checking a hand-written one from the corpus against the specification.
entries.noExample: a Python harness; run python3 tools/algo/check.py

entries.title: Memory checks of the emitted C
entries.what: tools/memcheck/memcheck.sh compiles every program of the named directories to C and builds it twice: with AddressSanitizer and UndefinedBehaviorSanitizer, and plainly with a memory report (what the array arena holds at exit, peak resident set, `leaks`). It writes one row per program. tools/memcheck/ci.sh is the gate: every program under the sanitizers, the leak probes (scale.sh, adversarial.sh: no row may grow with the loop length), the `parallel for` probes and the runtime fuzzers; `--quick` takes a few minutes.
entries.when: After a change to the C emitter, the runtime or ownership rules, before merging.
entries.noExample: a shell harness over whole directories; run tools/memcheck/ci.sh --quick

entries.title: Run a directory in three engines
entries.what: `tools/three-engines.sh DIR [names...]` runs every program in the interpreter, as C built natively, and as wasm from the direct backend in node, and requires every test to pass in each and the three outputs to agree byte for byte. A problem post's tests are meant to fail; for it only the agreement is required. tools/both-engines.sh is the same check without wasm, and `NO_C=1` skips C.
entries.when: On every directory a change touches, before committing: it is the check that a program means the same thing in every engine.
entries.noExample: a script over a directory; run tools/three-engines.sh DIR

entries.title: The golden snapshot of the corpus
entries.what: `tools/hub-golden.sh record DIR [paths]` writes, for every program of the corpus, its def hashes, AST, IR, C, the wasm module's sha256, and the output and exit status of the interpreter, the native build and the wasm build. `tools/hub-golden.sh compare A B` lists every difference between two snapshots and exits 1 if there is any.
entries.when: Around a compiler refactor that should change nothing: record before, record after, compare.
entries.noExample: a script over the whole corpus; run tools/hub-golden.sh record target/golden/NAME

entries.title: Time one program in every engine
entries.what: `tools/race-engines.sh prog.viv ...` times a program four ways (the interpreter compiled to wasm, the direct wasm backend, C through emcc to wasm, and native C), each around the run alone, best of RUNS, and checks that all four print the same. tools/bounds-cost.sh measures what the array bounds checks cost by building with and without `-DVIV_NO_BOUNDS`.
entries.when: To decide which engine a page or a job should use, or what a bounds check costs a hot loop.
entries.noExample: it takes timings; run tools/race-engines.sh bench/jacobi_stencil.viv

entries.title: A local viewer for branches in flight
entries.what: `node tools/viewer.mjs` serves http://localhost:4400, a code viewer that reads git on every request: every branch is a choice in the top bar and opens on the files it changed against main, each with its diff, highlighted as viv-lang.org highlights code.

entries.title: The feature catalog
entries.what: `viv features` prints what Viv has, by area: syntax, types, arrays, autodiff, correctness, the lenses, tools, performance, libraries, and the builtins, phrases, CLI verbs, lenses and modules read from the compiler's own tables. `viv features NAME` prints one feature (what it does, when to use it, an example and its output, the design doc, related features) or one area; `--search WORDS` ranks features by the words; `--json` prints the whole catalog as data. `--usage [paths]` counts how often each feature is used in the corpus, and lists the places where code does by hand what a feature provides.
entries.when: Before writing code: ask what Viv already does, instead of writing a loop, a getter or a sort that a feature replaces. After writing it: run `--usage` on the new code.
entries.noExample: it is this tool

entries.title: Release mode: select instead of verify
entries.what: A default (checked) run verifies: a contracted solve such as `spectrum_sym(A, vals)` runs two independent methods and stops on dissent, array accesses are bounds-checked, holds and `disjoint` pins are tested, and steps are recorded. `viv run --release` and a C build with `-DVIV_RELEASE` run the selected method alone and drop those checks. `release_mode()` says which build is running.
entries.when: Develop and test in the default mode; time and ship in release mode. `-DVIV_NO_BOUNDS` drops only the bounds checks.

example.code:
A = [[2.0, 1.0], [1.0, 2.0]]
vals = zeros(2)
spectrum_sym(A, vals)
show vals, release_mode()
test "the contracted solve gives the spectrum, ascending" {
    assert_allclose(vals, [1.0, 3.0], 1.0e-14)
}

entries.title: Fast mode: fused multiply-add, the platform libm and BLAS, checked against the exact engines
entries.what: `viv build --fast` compiles the same C with fused multiply-add (`-ffp-contract=fast`), the platform's libm for `exp`, `log`, `pow`, `sin` and the rest, and on macOS Accelerate for `@` on large finite operands and for `lin_solve`; `viv run --fast` builds and runs it. Its numbers differ from the exact engines' in the last bits. `viv check --fast` runs the interpreter and the exact C build (and the direct wasm with `--wasm`), requires them to agree byte for byte, runs the fast build, and compares the outputs number by number: text, integers and test results must be the same, and every other number within a stated tolerance (an ulp budget, widened by the condition number of the worst solve). The report names each number that differs, by how many ulps and what share of its tolerance; `--without contract,libm,blas` tells which freedom moves it. Exact stays the default everywhere, and the browser runs exact.
entries.when: Time and ship a long native run once `viv check --fast` passes on it. Develop, test and publish with the exact engines; a port's correctness is judged on them. Fast mode keeps the bounds checks; add `--release` to drop them as well.
entries.noExample: a fast build needs a C compiler; `viv check --fast scf/lock_water.viv` shows the report

entries.title: The cache-blocked `@`, with the plain loop's bits
entries.what: `A @ B` runs over blocks of `b` that stay in the cache and keeps tiles of four rows by eight columns of the result in registers. For each entry the terms are still added in the order of the inner index, with separate multiplies and adds, so the result is the same bit for bit as the plain i-p-j loop and the same in every engine. NumPy calls BLAS, which agrees to rounding.
entries.when: Write the product as `@` rather than a triple loop: the loop gives the same numbers and runs without the blocking.

example.output:
0
PASS the blocked product equals the i-p-j loop bit for bit

entries.title: GPU kernels, run by a CPU emulator that checks them
entries.what: `kernel def` declares a GPU kernel. One whose body is a single `return` of an elementwise expression (`return a * x + exp(z)`) is one thread per element, the tree fused. An explicit kernel uses `thread_id()`, `block_id()`, `block_size()`, `grid_size()`, `s = shared(N)` for a block's shared array and `barrier()`. Both are called like defs, `y = k(x, y)`, and the call returns the array parameters the kernel writes. The grid is 256 threads to a block and the blocks that cover the first array parameter, unless a top-level line `schedule k(blocks = 2, threads = 8)` gives it (an integer expression of literals, the kernel's Int parameters, `len` of its arrays and global constants; one per axis for a 2-D grid, gpu-2d-grids). Every engine runs a kernel as a loop over blocks and, between barriers, over threads (MCUDA), and stops with the block, thread, element and line on an index out of range, a shared element read before it is written, two threads touching one element with no barrier between, or two blocks touching one element. A barrier under a per-thread condition, a per-thread value kept across a barrier, allocation, strings, I/O and calls of defs are refused before the run. `viv cuda` writes the CUDA C.
entries.when: To write a kernel for a GPU and check it on a machine without one: its values in the emulator are the CPU's (a contract with `agree ... exactly` against the array code), and examples/cuda holds an elementwise tree, a `parallel for` and `sum` in the canonical order.

entries.title: 2-D grids for GPU kernels
entries.what: A kernel's grid can have two axes. `thread_id(1)`, `block_id(1)`, `block_size(1)` and `grid_size(1)` are the y axis (CUDA's `threadIdx.y` and the rest), `thread_id(0)` and `thread_id()` the x axis. A schedule key takes one value per axis, `threads = [32, 8]` and `blocks = [bx, by]`, and `cover = [w, h]` gives the index space the threads must cover, from which the blocks are derived (`(w + 32 - 1) // 32` along x); `cover` and `blocks` exclude each other. A thread of a stencil or a matrix product then has its column and row without dividing a flat index. The emulator numbers threads and blocks x first, as CUDA does, so every check (races, indices, shared memory) works as in 1-D; `viv cuda` launches with `dim3`.
entries.when: For kernels over a 2-D index space: stencils on a grid, matrix products, transposes.

example.output:
t: [0, 5, 10, 1, 6, 11, 2, 7, 12, 3, 8, 13, 4, 9, 14]
PASS the kernel equals transpose

entries.title: Arrays kept on the GPU across kernel calls: `on device`
entries.what: `on device u, v { ... }` keeps the named arrays on the device while the block runs: each is copied there once on entry and back once on exit, and kernel calls inside read and write them in place, so a time loop of launches makes no copies. `u, v = v, u` swaps two device buffers. Inside the block a named array may only be a kernel's array argument, a kernel's result (`v = k(u, v)`, the array the kernel writes), part of a swap, or `len(u)`; reading it on the host, a call of a def, `return`, and `break` out of the block are refused before the run, so no stale copy can be read. The arrays the names held before the block are not changed by it. `device_transfers()` is `[to device, to host, launches]` so far, the same in every engine; `viv cuda` writes the block as one host function with its copies at the two ends.
entries.when: For a time-stepping solver or any loop of kernel launches over the same arrays.

example.output:
u: [0, 0.75, 1.875, 2.5, 1.875, 0.75, 0]
[2, 2, 3]
PASS two arrays in, two out, one launch per step

entries.title: `parallel for`, checked for disjoint writes
entries.what: `parallel for i to n { }` runs its passes on several threads in a C build compiled with OpenMP, and in order everywhere else. Each pass may write a shared array only at elements indexed by `i` in one fixed position (`a[i]`, `m[i, j]`, `setslab(W, i, s)`, a def given `i` as the index it writes), or by `i` plus a constant (`a[i + 1]`, or `a[j]` after `j = i + 1` at the top of the pass), and may read a shared array it writes only there. A write two passes could share, a global written through a def, `break` and `return` are refused before the run in every engine, with the write named and a fix suggested. A scalar total is a reduction.
entries.when: For independent work per index (rows of a matrix, integrals per shell pair, samples) in a native build. Only the plain form: no `from`, `by` or `reversed`.

example.output:
a: [0, 1, 4, 9, 16, 25, 36, 49]
PASS each pass writes only its own element

entries.title: Pinning a `parallel for` as disjoint in the memory lens
entries.what: When the passes write different elements for a reason the compiler cannot see (a permutation, a list of unique pairs), a line `disjoint  parallel for i: out  "why"` under the def in the module's `.memory` file lets the loop compile. Every checked build records each element a pass writes and stops the run naming both passes if two write the same one; a release build trusts the pin.
entries.when: Instead of rewriting a scatter loop as a serial loop, after the compiler refuses it.

example.output:
out: [10, 30, 0, 20]
PASS a pinned loop writes through a permutation

entries.title: Each loop pass frees what it allocated
entries.what: In C and wasm, when a loop's body can allocate, the end of each pass frees everything allocated since the loop began except what the variables the body assigns hold now. A def returning a record keeps the record's arrays and frees the rest. The interpreter counts references, so all three engines run a loop of temporaries in bounded memory.
entries.when: Write temporaries inside the loop as plain expressions. Preallocating every array before the loop and passing it down as an output argument is no longer needed for memory.

example.code:
# every pass allocates x * 1.0 and r; at the end of each pass the compiled
# program frees what the pass made except what x and r hold now
x = ones(1000)
for step to 400 {
    x = x * 1.0
    r = x + 1.0
}
show sum(x), r[0]
test "a variable assigned in the loop keeps its array" {
    assert_near(sum(x), 1000.0, 0.0)
    assert_near(r[0], 2.0, 0.0)
}

entries.title: Native and wasm builds
entries.what: `viv prog.viv -o prog.c` writes portable C99 and `cc -std=c99 -O2 prog.c -lm` builds it; add `-fopenmp` (on macOS `-Xpreprocessor -fopenmp` with libomp) for `parallel for`, and `-DVIV_RELEASE` for a release build. `viv prog.viv -o prog.wasm` writes a wasm module directly. All three engines compute `sin`, `exp`, `pow` with Viv's own libm, so the outputs agree byte for byte.
entries.when: For runs longer than a few seconds: the interpreter walks the tree, and the compiled program runs the same code natively.
entries.noExample: a build needs a C compiler and writes files; tools/three-engines.sh shows the commands

entries.title: Each module compiled once, its object cached
entries.what: `viv build` writes the C as one translation unit per imported module (a large module in parts) and one for the program (`viv prog.viv --split <dir>`), compiles each unit once per distinct text, flags and compiler, and keeps the object under its SHA-256 in `~/.cache/viv` (or `$VIV_CACHE_DIR`); the next program that loads the module links the kept object. The exact build is `cc -O3`. The output is the one-file build's, byte for byte.
entries.when: Always, through `viv build`; `--single` builds one C file, `--no-cache` skips the cache, `--cache-clear` empties it.
entries.noExample: a build needs a C compiler and writes files; lang/viv/tests/split_build.rs runs one

entries.title: Function values compile by specialization
entries.what: A def or a lambda passed to a def is a value in the interpreter. For C and wasm the compiler specializes the callee per function argument (`apply_twice(triple, x)` becomes `apply_twice__triple(x)`), and lifts lambdas to defs, so the compiled code has only direct calls. A lambda passed to a def may read only its parameters, top-level names and defs, not the caller's locals.
entries.when: Pass a def where an algorithm takes a function (a root finder, an integrand, a key); the compiled call costs what a direct call costs.

example.output:
a: 18  b: 4
PASS a function value passed to a def is specialized for C and wasm

areas.heading: Libraries
areas.what: the Viv code a program can import

entries.title: Transformer pieces (lib/nn)
entries.what: The forward pass of each piece a transformer is made of, as whole-array expressions over the last axis, so each works on a sequence (T by D) or a batch (B by T by D): `rmsnorm`, `relu2` (ReLU squared), `softmax_rows`, causal `attention` (returning the output and the weights), `cross_entropy`, `embedding`. The backward passes come from `value_and_grad` over these defs; the tests hold the generated gradient of each piece to central differences. The hand-written adjoints are kept in lib/nn_adjoints as references.
entries.when: Building a neural network: use these instead of writing softmax or cross-entropy loops, and differentiate them with `value_and_grad` instead of writing a backward pass.

example.code:
# lib/nn: the forward pieces of a transformer, whole-array and batched.
from nn import cross_entropy, softmax_rows

logits = [[2.0, 0.0, 0.0], [0.0, 0.0, 3.0]]
P = softmax_rows(logits)
loss = cross_entropy(logits, [0.0, 2.0])
show P[0, :], loss
test "each row of a softmax sums to 1" {
    assert_allclose(sum(P, axis=-1), [1.0, 1.0], 1.0e-15)
}
test "cross-entropy is the mean of -log p of the targets" {
    assert_near(loss, -0.5 * (log(P[0, 0]) + log(P[1, 2])), 1.0e-15)
}

# SPDX-License-Identifier: MIT OR Apache-2.0
# SPDX-FileCopyrightText: 2026 The Viv authors

[0.786986, 0.106507, 0.106507]  loss: 0.167234

entries.title: Optimizers (lib/optim)
entries.what: SGD, SGD with momentum, Adam and Muon. For a model held as records of matrices, `adam_update` and `muon_update` update one matrix and its memories in place with the settings in an `AdamSettings` or `MuonSettings` record, and `for_leaves` applies them to every matrix of the model, as `opt.step()` does in PyTorch. The older flat form keeps the parameters in one vector with a lib/params layout and steps with `optim_step`; a test holds the two forms to the same bits.
entries.when: Training anything by gradient: write `for_leaves(adam_update, model, g, m, v, t + 1, 1.0, settings)` instead of an update loop per matrix.

PASS Adam reaches the minimum

entries.title: A small GPT (lib/gpt)
entries.what: A GPT in the shape of nanoGPT and the modded-nanogpt speedrun: token and position embeddings, blocks of RMSNorm, multi-head causal attention and a ReLU-squared MLP with residuals, and an output map. The model is a `Gpt` record holding an array of `Block` records; `train` runs the batch at once, takes the gradient with `value_and_grad` with respect to the whole model, and updates it with Muon on the blocks and Adam on the rest through `for_leaves`. A `GptConfig` record holds the sizes. lib/gpt/story_gpt trains one on a sentence and continues a prompt.
entries.when: As the reference for a model written as records, batched `@` and autodiff over records, and as a starting point for a language-model experiment.

example.code:
# lib/gpt: a small GPT as records of matrices, trained by value_and_grad,
# Muon and Adam. Here it learns a four-token cycle.
from gpt.gpt import Gpt, GptConfig, train

c = GptConfig { vocab: 4, context: 4, width: 8, layers: 1, hidden: 16, batch: 2 }
srand(1.0)
model = Gpt(c)
tokens = [0.0, 1.0, 2.0, 3.0, 0.0, 1.0, 2.0, 3.0, 0.0, 1.0, 2.0, 3.0]
STEPS = 30
losses = train(model, c, tokens, STEPS)
print("loss", fmt(losses[0], ".3f"), "->", fmt(losses[STEPS - 1], ".3f"))
test "training lowers the loss" {
    assert_lt(losses[STEPS - 1], 0.5 * losses[0])
}

entries.title: A model's parameters as one vector (lib/params)
entries.what: Keeps all of a model's matrices in one flat vector with a layout table beside it (the offset, rows and columns of each matrix): `param_table`, `param_declare`, `param_zeros`, `param_get`, `param_set`, `param_add`. It exists because `grad` once took only one flat array.

entries.title: Hartree-Fock quantum chemistry (lib/hf)
entries.what: Restricted, unrestricted and restricted-open Hartree-Fock on Gaussian basis sets, held against PySCF. `molecule("O 0 0 0; H ...", "6-31g")` (lib/hf/mole) builds a `Molecule` from text and a basis name, as PySCF's `gto.M` does; `rhf(mol)` (lib/hf/scf) runs the SCF and gives a record with the energy. lib/hf/hf runs the same pipeline with every integral stage cross-checked by its registry of methods (McMurchie-Davidson, Head-Gordon-Pople, Rys, Obara-Saika, Gauss-Hermite). entries.title: Computer algebra (lib/cas)
entries.what: A computer algebra system written in Viv: `cas("x^2 - 1")` parses text into a hash-consed expression store with exact rationals; `cas_diff`, `cas_expand`, `cas_definite` (a definite integral with a certificate verdict), `cas_text` (Viv source) and `cas_tex` (LaTeX). The compiler carries it, so `#! use lib/cas/cas` works from any directory, and `viv check --phrases` uses it to hold phrases to exact values.
entries.when: For an exact derivative, integral or simplification inside a program, or to print a formula as LaTeX.

example.code:
# lib/cas: exact symbolic algebra written in Viv.
import cas.cas as cas_module
from cas.calculus import cas_definite, cas_diff, cert_name
from cas.parse import cas
from cas.store import cas_sym
from cas.show import cas_tex, cas_text

x = cas_sym("x")
d = cas_diff(cas("x^3 - 2*x"), x)
big, area, verdict, why = cas_definite(cas("x^2"), x, cas("1"), cas("2"))
print("d/dx:", cas_text(d), " integral:", cas_text(area), " LaTeX:", cas_tex(area), " ", cert_name(verdict))
test "the integral of x^2 from 1 to 2 is exactly 7/3, and proved" {
    assert_true(cas_text(area) == "7 / 3")
    assert_true(cert_name(verdict) == "proved")
}

# SPDX-License-Identifier: MIT OR Apache-2.0
# SPDX-FileCopyrightText: 2026 The Viv authors

d/dx: 3 * x^2 - 2  integral: 7 / 3  LaTeX: \frac{7}{3}   proved
PASS the integral of x^2 from 1 to 2 is exactly 7/3, and proved

entries.title: MINPACK least squares (lib/minpack)
entries.what: A port of netlib MINPACK's Levenberg-Marquardt solver with a trust region: `lmder1` and `lmder`, with `lmpar`, `qrfac`, `qrsolv` and `enorm`, keeping the Fortran's arithmetic in its order so the iterates match a gfortran build of the original to the last bit (checked on the Moré-Garbow-Hillstrom problems by lib/minpack/mgh_check.viv). The residual function is a def `fcn(data, x, fvec, fjac, iflag)` that fills `fvec` or `fjac`. Every trial step writes a row of `hist`.
entries.when: Fitting a model to data by nonlinear least squares, instead of writing Gauss-Newton with a hand-tuned damping.

example.code:
# lib/minpack: MINPACK's lmder1 (Levenberg-Marquardt), here on Rosenbrock's
# residuals f = (10 (x1 - x0^2), 1 - x0), whose least-squares minimum is (1, 1).
from minpack.lmder import H_X, lmder1

def rosen(data: Arr, x: Arr, fvec: Arr, fjac: Arr, iflag) {
    if iflag == 1 {
        fvec[0] = 10.0 * (x[1] - x[0] * x[0])
        fvec[1] = 1.0 - x[0]
    }
    if iflag == 2 {
        fjac[0, 0] = -20.0 * x[0]
        fjac[0, 1] = 10.0
        fjac[1, 0] = -1.0
        fjac[1, 1] = 0.0
    }
    return iflag
}

x = [-1.2, 1.0]
fvec = zeros(2)
fjac = zeros(2, 2)
counts = zeros(2)
info = lmder1(rosen, [0.0], x, fvec, fjac, 1.0e-10, zeros(2), counts, zeros(1, H_X + 2))
show info, x, counts
test "lmder1 reaches (1, 1)" {
    assert_allclose(x, [1.0, 1.0], 1.0e-10)
}

entries.title: Randomized linear algebra (lib/randla)
entries.what: Sketching operators generated on the fly from Philox4x32-10 keyed by (seed, stream), so a sketch is the same in every engine (Gaussian, Rademacher, sparse sign SASO, subsampled randomized Hadamard), and the drivers built on them: the randomized range finder, QB and SVD with power iterations, Nystrom for PSD matrices, randomly pivoted Cholesky, sketch-and-precondition least squares (LSQR on A R^-1, to full accuracy), and the Hutchinson and Hutch++ trace estimators over an operator passed as a def.

# lib/randla: a rank-5 randomized SVD, from a sketch generated by Philox.

A = with_spectrum(60, 40, s, 1)

show sk[0], norm(A - (U * sk) @ Vt) / norm(s[5:])
test "the error is within 1% of the best rank-5 error" {
    assert_lt(norm(A - (U * sk) @ Vt), 1.01 * norm(s[5:]))
}

entries.title: Dense linear algebra (lib/schur, lib/svd, lib/polar, lib/lobpcg, lib/linalg)
entries.what: lib/schur: the real Schur form `A = Q T Q^T` by Householder reduction and Francis's double-shift QR, with a Sylvester solver for its blocks. lib/svd: the SVD by one-sided Jacobi (the algorithm of the `svd` builtin). lib/polar: Newton-Schulz orthogonalization, which Muon uses. lib/lobpcg: the lowest eigenpairs of an operator given as a def that applies it. lib/linalg: an inverse and a reproducible test matrix. Each has residual checks (`schur_residual`, `orthogonality`, `svd_residual`).
entries.when: For a decomposition the builtins do not give (Schur, polar, iterative eigenpairs of a matrix you never form). For a solve, an inverse, `eig_sym` or `svd`, use the builtins.

example.code:
# lib/schur: the real Schur form A = Q T Q^T by Householder and Francis's QR.
from schur import orthogonality, schur, schur_residual

A = [[4.0, 1.0, -2.0], [1.0, 2.0, 0.0], [-2.0, 3.0, 3.0]]
T = zeros(3, 3)
Q = zeros(3, 3)
schur(A, T, Q)
show schur_residual(A, T, Q), orthogonality(Q)
test "Q T Q^T gives A back, with Q orthogonal" {
    assert_lt(schur_residual(A, T, Q), 1.0e-14)
    assert_lt(orthogonality(Q), 1.0e-14)
}

entries.title: Control: LQR, Riccati, Lyapunov, balanced truncation (lib/lqr and others)
entries.what: lib/are solves the algebraic Riccati equation by the Schur method; lib/lqr is its front end for one input (`lqr_riccati`, `lqr_gains`, `lqr_residual`); lib/lyap solves the Lyapunov equation by Bartels and Stewart and gives controllability and observability Gramians and the H2 norm; lib/balance does balanced truncation. lib/cartpole and lib/chain are the plants: a cart-pole and a planar chain of rigid links (recursive Newton-Euler).
entries.when: Designing a controller or reducing a linear model, instead of integrating a Riccati ODE until it stops changing (lib/lqr keeps that method only to show how it fails).

example.code:
# lib/lqr: the LQR gains of the double integrator x'' = u, from the Riccati
# equation solved by the Schur method (lib/are). The exact gains are (1, sqrt(3)).
from lqr import lqr_gains, lqr_residual, lqr_riccati

A = [[0.0, 1.0], [0.0, 0.0]]
B = [[0.0], [1.0]]
P = lqr_riccati(A, B, eye(2), 1.0)
K = lqr_gains(P, B, 1.0)
show K, lqr_residual(P, A, B, eye(2), 1.0)
test "the gains are 1 and sqrt(3)" {
    assert_allclose(K, [1.0, sqrt(3.0)], 1.0e-12)
}

entries.title: Initial value problems, stiff and non-stiff (lib/ode)
entries.what: `ode_solve(rhs, jac, events, t0, t1, y0, p, cfg, t_eval, dirs, term)` integrates y' = rhs(t, y, p) by Dormand-Prince 5(4) (`DOPRI5`), Radau IIA of order 5 (`RADAU`), variable-order BDF (`BDF`), or `AUTO` (Dormand-Prince until Hairer's stiffness test fires, then Radau). Step-size control on rtol and atol as SciPy's solve_ivp does it (the same steps), dense output, events located on the dense output with direction and terminal flags, and `ode_batch` for many parameter sets on one grid. The rhs, its Jacobian and the events are defs passed as function values; an exact Jacobian is a def of `grad` rows (lib/ode/problems.viv), or `JAC_FD` takes forward differences. Python calls it as vp.ode.solve and vp.ode.batch.
entries.when: Instead of a hand-written RK4 loop with a fixed step, or a stiff problem stepped by an explicit method at the step its fastest mode allows.

example.code:
# lib/ode: Robertson's stiff kinetics to t = 40 by Radau IIA, with the exact
# Jacobian from grad (lib/ode/problems.viv); the published value of y1 at 40 is 0.7158271
from ode.solve import ode_cfg, ode_solve, no_events
from ode.core import RADAU, JAC_GIVEN
from ode.problems import robertson, robertson_jac

c = ode_cfg(RADAU, 40.0, 1.0e-8, 1.0e-12 * ones(3), 0.0, inf, 100000, JAC_GIVEN)
r = ode_solve(robertson, robertson_jac, no_events, 0.0, 40.0, [1.0, 0.0, 0.0], [0.04, 1.0e4, 3.0e7], c, [40.0], zeros(0), zeros(0))
y = r.y[0, :]
show y, r.nsteps
test "Robertson at t = 40" {
    assert_near(y[0], 0.7158270687, 1.0e-8)
    assert_near(sum(y), 1.0, 1.0e-12)
}

entries.title: Contracts and their registries (std/contracts)
entries.what: lang/viv/std/contracts.viv holds `integrate(f, a, b)` and `find_root(f, a, b)`: each runs every method in its registry (three quadratures: Gauss-Legendre, adaptive Simpson, Romberg; three bracketing root finders: bisection, Illinois, a safeguarded secant) and stops the run when two disagree, while `viv run --release` runs one. The methods are ordinary defs, a registry is an array of them (`[r_bisect, r_illinois, r_safe]`), and `sweep(methods, f, a, b)` cross-checks any registry. Bring it in with `#! use lang/viv/std/contracts` or `--use lang/viv/std/contracts.viv`; a phrase that needs one of these defs gets it added.
entries.when: For an integral or a root whose answer you want checked by methods from different families, and as the pattern for a registry of your own methods.

example.code:
# std/contracts: integrate and find_root run their default method (Gauss, the
# safeguarded secant); `using every method` runs all three and stops the run
# when one disagrees with their median.
from lang.viv.std.contracts import find_root, integrate

area = integrate(fn(x) -> exp(-x * x), 0.0, 1.0)
root = find_root(fn(x) -> cos(x) - x, 0.0, 1.0)
print(fmt(area, ".12f"), fmt(root, ".12f"))
test "three quadratures agree on the integral" {
    all_area = integrate(fn(x) -> exp(-x * x), 0.0, 1.0) using every method
    assert_near(area, 0.746824132812427, 1.0e-12)
    assert_near(all_area, area, 1.0e-12)
}
test "three root finders agree on the root" {
    all_root = find_root(fn(x) -> cos(x) - x, 0.0, 1.0) using every method
    assert_near(cos(root), root, 1.0e-14)
    assert_near(all_root, root, 1.0e-14)
}
